summary: Henri Seyrig was an archaeologist and historian who studied at the University of Paris around 1919–1922 and taught Daniel Schlumberger. He later served as director of the Institut français du Proche-Orient from around 1946 to 1967.
Henri d'Ollone worked in sinology and tibetology. He received his military education at the École spéciale militaire de Saint-Cyr between circa 1887 and 1889.

Henri de Lubac was a religious and Buddhist studies scholar who earned a Dr.theol. at the Pontifical Gregorian University. He taught at Théologat de Fourvière (~1929–1950) and served as a professor at the Catholic University of Lyon (1929–1961).

Indologist Henriette Johanna Wilhelmina Salomons earned her B.A. at Leiden under Christianus Cornelis Uhlenbeck (1901) and her Ph.D. at Utrecht under Willem Caland (~1906–1913). She was a lecturer of Dutch at the University of Copenhagen (1928–1929).

Linguist Henrik Barić studied at Graz under Rudolf Meringer (~1906–1908) and earned his Ph.D. at Vienna (~1908–1912). He served as professor at the University of Belgrade (1920–1954), later joining Sarajevo University and directing the Institute of Balkan Studies (~1954–1957).

Henrik Samuel Nyberg, a scholar of Iranian, central Asian, linguistics, and religion, completed his Ph.D. at Uppsala (1908–1919) under Johansson, Zetterstéen, Danielsson, and Persson. He later served as docent and professor of Semitic languages at Uppsala (1919; 1931–1956).

Henrik Zilliacus was a scholar of linguistics, history, and archaeology. He studied at the University of Helsinki from circa 1926 to 1936, later held a post there around 1944–1974, and taught Klaus Karttunen.

Henry Alfred Whitehead was an indologist and religious studies scholar who studied at Trinity College, Oxford (~1873–1877). He later served as principal of Bishop's College, Calcutta, from around 1883 to 1899.

Henry Baily Wade Garrick was an indologist and archaeologist educated at the Royal College of Art. He served as Cunningham's assistant at the Archaeological Survey of India (1880–1890) and worked as an artist for the Geological Survey of India (1891–1911).

Indologist and historian Henry Beveridge studied at Queen's University Belfast (1856) and the University of Glasgow (~1853–1857). He worked for the Indian Civil Service (1857–1893) and served as president of The Asiatic Society (1890–1891).
Henry Bower, a scholar of Indology and linguistics, studied at Vepery Seminary. He later served as the principal Tamil examiner at the University of Madras from around 1872 to 1879.

Henry Chung-hung Shiu, a scholar of Buddhist studies and philosophy, earned his Ph.D. from the University of Toronto (2006) and studied under Shek-Wing Tam, Priestley, Waterhouse, and Oxtoby. He held a post at Emmanuel College, Toronto.

Henry Clarke Warren worked in Buddhist studies and Indology, studying at Harvard, Johns Hopkins, and Oxford under Palmer, Greenough, Lanman, Bloomfield, and Rhys Davids. He founded the Pali Text Society and the Harvard Oriental Series (1891).

Henry Cousens was an archaeologist and Indologist. He worked at the Archaeological Survey of India, serving as an assistant to Cunningham in 1881 and later as Superintendent of Western India from 1891 to 1910.

Henry Creswicke Rawlinson, educated at Great Ealing School and Middlesex University, worked in Iranian and Central Asian archaeology and history. He served in the East India Company, the Foreign Office, and as director of the Royal Asiatic Society (1862–1895).

Henry Drummond Williamson was an Indologist and linguist who studied at Corpus Christi College, University of Cambridge (~1874–1889). He served as a missionary with the Church Missionary Society from 1877 to 1893.

Henry George Briggs was an Indologist and historian. He held posts as assistant secretary at the Great Indian Peninsula Railway (1856), secretary to the Bombay Municipal Corporation (1860–1862), and worked for the Public Works Department.

Henry George Keene studied at Fort William College, Wadham College, Sidney Sussex College, and East India Company College. An Indologist and Iranian scholar, he served the East India Company and was professor of Arabic and Persian at EICC (1824–1834).

Indologist and historian Henry Green served as headmaster of the English School, Surat (1841) and as Professor of Political Economy and Literature at Deccan College (1837–1857). He also held posts at Elphinstone College and the Parsee Benevolent Institution.

Henry Hamilton Hadley studied at Yale and Andover Theological Seminary. A scholar of religious studies and linguistics, he held Hebrew professorships at Yale Divinity School (1861), Union Theological Seminary (1862), and Yale University (~1862–1864).
